as_read: Leucine alone did not improve muscle mass or strength in pooled RCTs; two small positive trials and two favorable reviews leave the evidence conflicting with no clear benefit.

quote.text: Leucine-isolated supplementation did not improve muscle mass and strength in elderly.

proposed_decision_text: A meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found leucine alone had no effect on lean mass, handgrip or leg press in older adults (PMID 35845777). Free leucine added nothing to resistance training in young men (PMID 32079916), frail older women (PMID 40926079) or midlife women (PMID 31577520). Two small trials are positive: walking time in institutionalized older adults on 6 g/day (PMID 32230954) and fat-free mass during energy restriction on 3 g/day (PMID 37923932). An umbrella review favors leucine for muscle mass in sarcopenia without saying in its abstract whether that is free leucine (PMID 32483625), and a 2025 meta-analysis calls its evidence low quality and limited when leucine is used alone (PMID 40805998). The stored trials tested an amino acid mixture (PMID 16507602) and a whey drink (PMID 24284442), measuring protein synthesis over hours. The evidence conflicts with no clear benefit for the free leucine on these labels.

studies_to_add.quote: The use of l-leucine supplementation can have some beneficial effects on sarcopenia and could be considered for the treatment of sarcopenia in older individuals.

stored_rating_note: Stored positive_strong study ratings on 16507602 and 24284442 are acute synthesis results on a mixture and a whey drink. 16507602 is indexed as a controlled clinical trial, and its abstract doesn't state randomization, though stored as rct. The stored applicability text says the umbrella review found no benefit in healthy older adults and for strength and performance; the abstract read doesn't say this.
